_meta.title: Act 1 chartable time series — the raw arrays
_meta.phase: 0 (series harvest pass, added after the initial verification pass)
_meta.purpose: history-series.json holds verified VALUES and the annotations/caveats that must ship with them. THIS file holds the chartable ARRAYS. Phase 1 draws from here; it reads history-series.json for what each line means and what must be said alongside it.
_meta.format: Each series is {label, unit, definition, source, url, published, tier, quote, coverage, caveats, data}. `data` is [[x, y], ...] with x = year unless stated. Nulls are absent observations, never zeros.
hard_rules: Where a series has TWO variants (capital gains statutory vs effective; top-1% share with vs without capital gains; union density on two denominators), BOTH are stored and the chart must label which it plots. Silently picking one is a correctness bug.
Series with `projections_begin` must render projections visually distinct from actuals, or not render them at all.
Series marked `derived: true` are OUR arithmetic on fetched inputs, not published figures. The inputs are stored alongside. Label them as derivations in the methodology page.

top_statutory_rate.label: Top marginal individual income tax rate
top_statutory_rate.definition: Highest statutory marginal rate on ordinary individual income. TPC's own disclaimer must ship with the chart: the series 'contains a number of simplifications and ignores factors such as income thresholds or deduction values'.
top_statutory_rate.source: Tax Policy Center, Historical Highest Marginal Income Tax Rates
top_statutory_rate.caveats: 2024-2026 are NOT from the TPC PDF (which ends 2023) — 2024-2025 from Tax Foundation historical brackets, 2026 from IRS IR-2025-103. Flag the join. Four TPC/Tax Foundation conflicts remain unresolved: 1922 (58 vs 56), 1934-35 (63 vs 70), 1970 (71.75 vs 70), 2003 (35 vs 38.6).

payroll_cap.label: Social Security taxable maximum (the wage cap)
payroll_cap.definition: Annual maximum of an individual's covered earnings subject to the OASDI portion of FICA/SECA, nominal dollars, per worker per employer. Does NOT cap the Medicare/HI portion, which has been uncapped since 1994. Indexed to the national average wage index, not prices; no increase in a year following no COLA.
payroll_cap.source: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base
payroll_cap.quote: Amounts for 1937-74 and for 1979-81 were set by statute; all other amounts were determined under automatic adjustment provisions
payroll_cap.caveats: SSA publishes the first six entries as ranges (1937-50, 1951-54, 1955-58, 1959-65, 1966-67, 1968-71); expanded here to one row per year at the constant published value. Flat spans 2009-2011 ($106,800) and 2015-2016 ($118,500) are no-COLA years, as published, not errors.
payroll_cap.chart_note: THIS IS THE 'QUIET REGRESSIVE CLIMB' SERIES. Its power comes from pairing it with average or top incomes: the cap rose ~61x nominally since 1937 while top incomes rose far more, so an ever-smaller share of total earnings sits below it. Consider plotting the cap as a share of the top 1% income threshold.

payroll_rate_combined.label: Combined payroll tax rate (employee + employer)
payroll_rate_combined.definition: Statutory FICA rate, employee + employer combined, as a percent of taxable earnings. OASDI applies only up to the cap; HI is uncapped since 1994. EXCLUDES the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax (2013+), which SSA states is 'not reflected in the tax rates shown in the table'.
payroll_rate_combined.source: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Social Security & Medicare Tax Rates
payroll_rate_combined.caveats: Rate shown is not always the rate paid: 1984 employee credit of 0.3pp (effective 5.4%); SECA credits 1984-89; 2011-2012 employee OASDI cut of 2.0pp (effective employee rate 4.2%). Those temporary reductions are NOT in this array.

additional_medicare_tax.quote: Beginning in 2013, an additional HI tax of 0.9 percent is assessed on earned income exceeding $125,000 for each married individual filing separately, $200,000 for individuals filing as single, and $250,000 for married couples filing jointly.

capital_gains_effective.label: Top long-term capital gains rate — EFFECTIVE
capital_gains_effective.definition: EFFECTIVE maximum marginal federal rate on long-term capital gains for a high-income individual. Folds in the pre-1987 partial exclusion, pre-1987 and 1991-97 alternative tax rates, the 1970-78 minimum tax, the 1979-96 AMT, the 1968-70 Vietnam surcharge, the Pease phaseout, and the 3.8% NIIT from 2013. NOT the headline statutory rate.
capital_gains_effective.source: Tax Foundation, Federal Capital Gains Tax Collections, Historical Data
capital_gains_effective.quote: The maximum tax rate includes effects of exclusions (1954-1986), alternative tax rates (1954-1986; 1991-1996), the minimum tax (1970-1978), alternative minimum tax (1979-1996), income tax surcharges (1968-1970), the Pease limitation (1991-1998, 2013-2017), and the 3.8% net investment income tax of (2013-present).
capital_gains_effective.caveats: Four midyear rate changes shown as split values in the source — 1978, 1981, 1997, 2003. This array uses the LATER (post-change) value for those years and records the pair in `split_years`. No 2026 value published by this source; use the statutory series for 2026.

capital_gains_statutory.label: Top long-term capital gains rate — STATUTORY
capital_gains_statutory.definition: Headline maximum statutory rate on individual long-term capital gains. Excludes AMT, surtaxes, phaseouts, and the 3.8% NIIT by the source's own disclaimer.
capital_gains_statutory.source: Wolters Kluwer, Historical Capital Gains Rates
capital_gains_statutory.corroborating_quote: The maximum statutory rate on long-term gains was 28% starting 1991, 20% starting May 1997, 15% starting May 2003 and 20% starting in 2013. — Tax Policy Center
capital_gains_statutory.caveats: The 1934-35 and 1936-37 figures assume a 10-year holding period and are therefore already effective-style, not clean statutory. Diverges from the effective series in 1970-78 (surcharge + minimum tax) and from 2013 (NIIT).
capital_gains_statutory.why_two_series: THE TOOL MUST PICK ONE AND SAY WHICH. The effective series is more honest about what people paid; the statutory series is what a policy slider actually changes. Recommendation: plot the STATUTORY series in Act 1 (it is the policy lever) and use the effective series as the second line in the same 'gap between law and reality' pattern used for the top income tax rate.

estate_tax.label: Federal estate tax — exemption and top rate
estate_tax.definition: Exemption = nominal-dollar amount of a decedent's estate shielded from federal estate tax by year of death. Legal name changed over time: straight exemption pre-1977; unified credit / applicable exclusion 1977-2010; basic exclusion amount 2011-present, PORTABLE to a surviving spouse since 2011 (so a married couple's effective shield is 2x). Top rate = highest marginal rate above the top bracket.

sources.title: IRS SOI, The Estate Tax: Ninety Years and Counting

estate_tax.caveats: 2010 IS THE REPEAL YEAR AND MUST BE FLAGGED VISUALLY. EGTRRA repealed the estate tax for 2010; the December 2010 Tax Relief Act retroactively reinstated it at $5,000,000/35% but let 2010 estates ELECT OUT — no estate tax in exchange for carryover rather than stepped-up basis. Also: the 1987-2001 top EFFECTIVE rate reached 60% for estates in a specific range because a 5% surtax phased out the graduated-rate benefit; the 55% statutory figure understates the true marginal rate in that bubble.
estate_tax.chart_note: STRONGEST ANNOTATION IN THIS SERIES: the $60,000 exemption held FLAT for 34 years, 1942-1976. Inflation did the repealing that Congress did not.

estate_returns.label: Estate tax returns filed and taxable, by filing year
estate_returns.definition: Form 706 returns FILED in the stated calendar year, all gross-estate sizes. FILING YEAR, NOT YEAR OF DEATH — most returns in year T are for deaths in T-1, so the series lags exemption changes by about a year. 'Taxable' = returns with positive net estate tax after credits.
estate_returns.source: Tax Policy Center, reproducing IRS SOI Estate Tax Returns Study Table 1
estate_returns.quote: Number of Estate Tax Returns Filed and Share of Returns Taxable by Size of Gross Estate, Filing Years 2001-2022
estate_returns.caveats: The taxable COUNT is DERIVED (total x percent taxable), because the source publishes total returns and percent taxable, not a count. Validation: derived 2019 = 2,570, matching Tax Foundation's IRS-sourced 2,570 exactly; derived 2021 = 2,586 vs Tax Foundation 2,584 (rounding). SOI figures are sample-based estimates. The 2011 trough reflects the 2010 repeal; the 2019-2020 drop reflects the 2018 TCJA doubling plus COVID-era IRS processing disruption.
estate_returns.extension_note: Filing years 2023 and 2024 added 2026-08-17 from IRS SOI estate Table 1 primary files (23es01fy.xlsx, 24es01fy.xlsx). For those two years the taxable count is IRS's OWN figure, not derived: FY2023 9,024 filed / 3,690 taxable; FY2024 7,195 filed / 2,663 taxable. The pct_taxable column is null for them because the count came direct. B9 CLOSED.

receipts_pct_gdp.label: Federal receipts as a percent of GDP
receipts_pct_gdp.definition: OMB fiscal-year federal budget receipts divided by calendar-year nominal GDP, x100. A HYBRID RATIO — numerator is fiscal year, denominator calendar year. Constructed by the St. Louis Fed, not a primary OMB publication.
receipts_pct_gdp.quote: The series was constructed by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis in January 2013 using the formula: FYFRGDA188S = ((FYFR/1000)/GDPA)*100
receipts_pct_gdp.resolves: THIS CLOSES THE DOSSIER'S UNSOURCED '14.5-20%' RANGE CLAIM. Verified post-1945 bounds: MINIMUM 13.16% (1950); MAXIMUM 19.81% (1945). Excluding the 1945 demobilization year, the maximum is 19.76% (2000). The honest published range is roughly 13.2% to 19.8% of GDP, NOT 14.5-20%.
receipts_pct_gdp.caveats: Do not present as a smooth line without noting the WWII spike. The 'Hauser's law' flatness argument should be made on the post-1950 portion, and must carry the composition-shift caveat (see receipts_by_source).

outlays_pct_gdp.label: Federal net outlays as a percent of GDP
outlays_pct_gdp.definition: OMB fiscal-year federal net outlays divided by calendar-year nominal GDP, x100. Same hybrid construction as receipts_pct_gdp, so the two are directly comparable and their difference is the deficit on this basis.

receipts_by_source.label: Federal receipts by source, percent of total receipts
receipts_by_source.definition: Percent of total UNIFIED-budget receipts (on-budget + off-budget), fiscal year. 'Payroll' = social insurance and retirement receipts: OASDI and HI payroll taxes, unemployment insurance, federal employee retirement, railroad retirement — the great majority is off-budget Social Security payroll tax. 'Other' = estate and gift + customs duties + miscellaneous (chiefly Federal Reserve earnings). Each row sums to 100.
receipts_by_source.source: OMB Historical Tables, Table 2.2, FY2025 Budget vintage, reproduced by Tax Policy Center
receipts_by_source.quote: Source: Office of Management and Budget, Historical Tables, Table 2.2; http://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/budget/Historicals/ (last accessed May 20, 2024).
receipts_by_source.why_this_matters: THIS IS THE SERIES THAT CARRIES THE REGRESSIVITY ARGUMENT, and the top-rate chart alone conceals it. In the verified actuals: corporate fell from 32.1% (FY1952) to 9.4% (FY2023) while payroll rose from 9.7% to 36.4% over the same span, and excise collapsed from 13.4% to 1.7%. The corporate share did not vanish — the payroll tax, which is capped and regressive, took its place.
receipts_by_source.caveats: Projections for 2024-2029 exist in the source and are EXCLUDED from this array — OMB's FY2025 projection put corporate at 12.2% for FY2025, while the CBO actual implies ~8.6%. Never present a projection as history. Definitional breaks: 1937 (Social Security payroll tax begins), and the July-September 1976 transition quarter, which is a 3-month period and is excluded here.
receipts_by_source.fy2024_fy2025_note: OMB's own FY2024/FY2025 actuals exist only in hist02z2_fy2027.xlsx (blocked). CBO's Monthly Budget Review gives dollar levels on DIFFERENT categories (customs broken out; excise folded into 'other'), so they cannot be appended: FY2024 individual $2,426B / payroll $1,709B / corporate $530B / customs $77B / other $176B; FY2025 $2,656B / $1,748B / $452B / $195B / $183B.

corporate_top_rate.label: Top federal corporate income tax rate
corporate_top_rate.definition: Highest statutory marginal corporate rate. Calendar/tax year, NOT fiscal year — do not co-plot on a fiscal-year axis without noting this.
corporate_top_rate.source: Tax Foundation, Historical US Federal Corporate Income Tax Rates & Brackets, 1909-2025 (sourced to IRS SOI Historical Table 24 for 1909-2010 and Form 1120 instructions for 2011-2025)
corporate_top_rate.caveats: 1987 is a BLENDED TRANSITION YEAR under TRA86 — label it as such, do not plot 34%. The 1988-92 and 1993-2017 schedules contain 'bubble' rates (39% and 38%) that exceed the nominal top rate for a band of income; the nominal top rate understates the true marginal rate there. 1940 needs re-verification against IRS Historical Table 24 (two overlapping schedules did not survive conversion).

top_income_share_wid.label: Top 1% and top 0.1% share of PRE-TAX national income (WID / DINA basis)
top_income_share_wid.definition: WID pretax NATIONAL income (sptinc), EQUAL-SPLIT ADULTS (income split equally within couples; unit = adult aged 20+, NOT tax units). Pretax = after the pension and unemployment insurance system (social insurance benefits INCLUDED, other transfers not), before income taxes. National income INCLUDES undistributed corporate profits, imputed rents, and imputed taxes — it is NOT the classic Piketty-Saez 'fiscal income' series.
top_income_share_wid.source: WID.world, via Our World in Data grapher CSV
top_income_share_wid.route_note: wid.world/bulk_download/ returns 404 and api.wid.world returns 403. Saez's own update is .xlsx. The OWID grapher CSV endpoint is the working route, and REQUIRES csvType=filtered FIRST in the query string plus tab=chart — without tab=chart you get only the map year.
top_income_share_wid.caveats: MUST BE LABELED AS THE WID/NATIONAL-INCOME VARIANT. It is not interchangeable with the Piketty-Saez fiscal-income series stored separately, nor with Auten-Splinter. Three series, three definitions, three different levels for the same year. The 2023 and 2024 observations are flagged as extrapolated in the source.

top_income_share_auten_splinter.label: Top 1% income share — Auten & Splinter (the competing series)
top_income_share_auten_splinter.source: Auten & Splinter, Income Inequality in the United States: Extensions and Updates, Table A1
top_income_share_auten_splinter.definition: Same national-income denominator as WID but a different allocation of underreported income, retirement income, and corporate profit — which is why its top 1% pre-tax level runs about 5 points below WID's.
top_income_share_auten_splinter.headline_quote: after-tax top income shares declined in the late 1960s and increased in the late 1980s and 1990s. However, after-tax top income shares are little changed relative to the early 1960s.
top_income_share_auten_splinter.chart_requirement: PLOT AGAINST WID, BOTH LABELED, NEVER AVERAGED. Two credible tax-data series differ by ~8 points on the same year (2022: WID/Saez 23.6% incl. capital gains vs Auten-Splinter 15.5%). Direction is shared; magnitude is genuinely contested. This is causal-honesty note #6.
top_income_share_auten_splinter.note_on_scale: Source publishes these as decimal fractions (0.104); converted to percent here (10.4) to match the other two series.

piketty_saez_effective_rates.label: Effective TOTAL federal tax rate by top income group, 1960-2004
piketty_saez_effective_rates.source: Piketty & Saez, How Progressive is the U.S. Federal Tax System?, JEP 21(1) 2007
piketty_saez_effective_rates.coverage: Totals for 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2004 across 11 income groups; COMPONENTS broken out for 1970 and 2004 only
piketty_saez_effective_rates.definition: TOTAL federal rate across four taxes — individual income + payroll + corporate income + estate and gift — with corporate and estate taxes IMPUTED to individuals as owners. These are not taxes the filer writes a check for. Income base excludes government transfers.
piketty_saez_effective_rates.why_it_matters: This is the tool's central honesty exhibit. Statutory top rate in 1960: 91%. Total effective rate on the top 0.01%: over 70%. Individual income tax portion alone: 31%. And most of the subsequent fall to ~35% came from the collapse of the imputed CORPORATE and ESTATE components, not the individual income tax — which fell only ~31% to ~26%. A tool that says 'the rich used to pay 91%' is wrong; one that says 'the rich used to pay a much higher TOTAL federal rate, mostly through corporate and estate taxes that have since shrunk' is right, and more interesting.
piketty_saez_effective_rates.components_note: Component breakdowns (individual income / payroll / corporate / estate) exist for 1970 and 2004 only, and are in the harvest transcript. The 2004 top-0.01% row reads: individual income 26.2, payroll 1.4, corporate 2.5, estate 4.6, total 34.7.

cbo_effective_rates_historical.label: CBO effective federal tax rates by income group, 1979-2005, and rates+shares by component 1979-2002

sources.title: CBO, Historical Effective Federal Tax Rates: 1979 to 2005
CBO, Historical Effective Federal Tax Rates: 1979 to 2002
sources.coverage: 24 points x 9 groups x 5 rate measures and 5 share measures

cbo_effective_rates_historical.breakthrough: THIS PARTIALLY BREAKS BLOCKER B4. CBO's older reports publish the quintile series as extractable PDF tables — total effective rate, and separately the individual income / social insurance / corporate / excise components, plus SHARE of total federal tax liabilities by group. The dossier's claim that this data was only available in spreadsheets was true only for the post-2002 vintages.
cbo_effective_rates_historical.still_missing: 2003-2021 shares and rates remain .xlsx-only. Series 4a (to 2005) and 4b (to 2002) are the longest non-spreadsheet CBO series obtainable.
cbo_effective_rates_historical.caveats: Negative individual-income-tax rates and shares for the lowest quintile from 1987 onward are refundable credits (EITC, later CTC), not errors.

by_component_and_shares_1979_2002.groups_note: Each table maps group name -> 24 annual values, 1979 through 2002 in order.

top_1pct_wealth_share.label: Share of total household net worth held by the top 1%
top_1pct_wealth_share.definition: Share of total U.S. household-sector net worth held by households in the 99th-100th wealth percentile. NET WORTH, not income.
top_1pct_wealth_share.source: Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts via FRED series WFRBST01134
top_1pct_wealth_share.coverage: 1989Q3-2026Q1 quarterly, 147 points; annual Q4 series 1989-2025 stored below
top_1pct_wealth_share.caveats: The DFA is a MODEL-BASED INTERPOLATION — it distributes Financial Accounts aggregates using triennial Survey of Consumer Finances microdata, so quarterly movements between SCF waves are interpolated, not measured. The whole series revises when a new SCF wave lands. Date-stamp any figure taken from it.

real_median_household_income.label: Real median household income
real_median_household_income.definition: Median annual money income of all U.S. households, inflation-adjusted. Deflator is SPLICED: C-CPI-U for 2000-2024, R-CPI-U-RS pre-2000. Money income BEFORE taxes, EXCLUDING noncash benefits and capital gains.
real_median_household_income.source: Census Bureau CPS ASEC via FRED series MEHOINUSA672N
real_median_household_income.quote: Income in 2024 C-CPI-U (2000-2024) and R-CPI-U-RS (pre-2000) adjusted dollars.
real_median_household_income.caveats: SERIES BEGINS 1984 — there is no earlier data in this series, so it cannot support a '1950s vs today' comparison. MAJOR BREAK at 2013/2014 (CPS ASEC income-question redesign, split sample) and a further processing change in 2017; the 2019 jump ($77,700 to $83,260) is unusually large and partly a collection artifact. 2020-21 estimates are affected by pandemic-era CPS nonresponse. 2025 data expected ~September 2026.
real_median_household_income.record_caveat: The 2024 value is the highest on record BUT Census states it is 'not statistically different from the 2023 estimate of $82,690'. Qualify the word 'record' or drop it.

real_gdp_growth.label: Real GDP growth, annual
real_gdp_growth.definition: BEA's PUBLISHED annual real GDP growth rate — percent change from the preceding year. These are BEA's own chain-weighted figures, NOT arithmetic on rounded levels.
real_gdp_growth.caveats: Will not exactly reproduce a naive percent change computed off rounded level data. Note the vintage differs slightly from the GDP level series (2026-03-13 vs 2026-04-09).
real_gdp_growth.chart_use: This is the series for the 'decade growth vs top rate' comparison. USE IT WITH CAUSAL-HONESTY NOTES 1, 2 AND 3 ATTACHED — the correlation between top rates and growth is the single most abused chart in tax politics, in both directions.

spm_poverty.label: Supplemental Poverty Measure, overall rate
spm_poverty.definition: Percent of the population with resources below the SPM threshold. SPM counts POST-tax, POST-transfer resources (SNAP, housing subsidies, EITC and refundable credits, WIC, LIHEAP) net of necessary expenses (taxes, work expenses, child care, medical out-of-pocket), against geographically-adjusted thresholds.
spm_poverty.source: U.S. Census Bureau, CPS ASEC — assembled from year-by-year Census reports and press releases
spm_poverty.why_it_matters: THE MOST DEFENSIBLE CLAIM THE TOOL CAN MAKE. Poverty fell to a record low DURING a recession because of transfers (9.1% in 2020, 7.8% in 2021), then snapped back ~4.6 points when they lapsed (12.4% in 2022). At the margin, US poverty is a policy choice about transfers, not purely a labor-market outcome.
spm_poverty.caveats: THE SPM IS REVISED AND IS NOT A CONSISTENT TIME SERIES. Census itself warns 'Comparisons over time should be made with caution.' Two documented conflicts: 2015 printed as 14.3 in the 2015 report but 14.5 in the 2016 report; 2019 printed as 11.7 in the 2019 report but 11.8 in a 2023 Census story. Method breaks at 2013 (CPS ASEC redesign), 2017 (processing change), and 2020-21 (pandemic nonresponse). 2009 and 2010 could not be retrieved — those reports live only on www2.census.gov, which is robots-disallowed.
spm_poverty.data_note: 2015 uses the restated 14.5 and 2019 the restated 11.8, for internal consistency with the later vintages. Both original values are recorded in the caveats above.

healthcare_pct_gdp.label: National health expenditures as a share of GDP
healthcare_pct_gdp.blocker: CMS publishes the complete 1960-2024 annual series only as ZIP archives of Excel workbooks ('NHE Summary, including share of GDP, CY 1960-2024'). No CSV, no HTML table, no PDF with the full series.
healthcare_pct_gdp.definition: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts total divided by current-dollar GDP.
healthcare_pct_gdp.caveats: TWO NCHS VINTAGES DISAGREE for the same years because of GDP and NHEA benchmark revisions (2000: 13.3% vs 13.4%; 2015: 17.7% vs 17.6%). CMS lists benchmark revisions for 2004, 2009, 2014, 2019 and 2024. Do not mix vintages within one chart line.

alternative_full_series.label: WHO current health expenditure as % of GDP — DIFFERENT DEFINITION, do not splice
alternative_full_series.warning: WHO 'current health expenditure' EXCLUDES capital investment and some administration that CMS NHE includes, so it runs roughly 1.0-1.5 points BELOW the CMS share. Never splice it onto the CMS numbers.

per_capita_2024.quote: NHE grew 7.2% to $5.3 trillion in 2024, or $15,474 per person, and accounted for 18.0% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

public_college_tuition.label: Published tuition and fees, public four-year institutions, constant dollars
public_college_tuition.definition: Average undergraduate tuition and required fees, public 4-year institutions, institution-reported, in constant 2023-24 dollars (NCES deflates with CPI-U on a July-June school-year basis). UNWEIGHTED institutional average, not enrollment-weighted.
public_college_tuition.source: NCES Digest of Education Statistics, Table 330.10
public_college_tuition.quote: Average undergraduate tuition, fees, room, and board rates charged for full-time students in degree-granting postsecondary institutions, by level and control of institution: Selected academic years, 1963-64 through 2023-24
public_college_tuition.resolves: THIS REPLACES THE DOSSIER'S UNSOURCED 'TUITION TRIPLED 1980-2020' CLAIM, and corrects its direction. Real published tuition PEAKS at 2015-16 ($11,405) and falls ~13% through 2023-24 ($9,872). A series truncated at 2019-20 would be cherry-picked near the peak. From 1980-81 ($2,872) to 2015-16 ($11,405) real published tuition roughly QUADRUPLED, then declined.
public_college_tuition.critical_pairing: PUBLISHED PRICE IS NOT NET PRICE. College Board: average NET tuition and fees for first-time full-time in-state students at public four-years peaked in 2012-13 at $4,450 (2025 dollars) and fell to an estimated $2,300 in 2025-26 — a ~48% real decline. Showing published price alone tells the opposite story from showing net price alone. THE TOOL MUST SHOW BOTH OR NEITHER.
public_college_tuition.data_note: Year label is the FIRST year of the academic year (1963 = 1963-64).

net_price_series.label: College Board: published vs NET tuition and fees, public four-year in-state, 2025 dollars
net_price_series.quote: After adjusting for inflation, the average net tuition and fees paid by first-time full-time in-state students enrolled in public four-year institutions peaked in 2012-13 at $4,450 (in 2025 dollars) and declined to an estimated $2,300 in 2025-26.
net_price_series.caveat: Levels NOT comparable to the NCES series above — College Board is enrollment-weighted and in-state; NCES is an unweighted institutional average; and the constant-dollar base years differ (2025 vs 2023-24).

productivity_pay_gap.label: Net productivity vs typical worker hourly compensation, index 1948Q1=100
productivity_pay_gap.definition: Two indexes, both 1948Q1 = 100, both inflation-adjusted. Net productivity = growth of output of goods and services less depreciation, per hour worked. Typical worker compensation = inflation-adjusted hourly compensation of production/nonsupervisory workers.
productivity_pay_gap.source: Economic Policy Institute, The Productivity-Pay Gap
productivity_pay_gap.caveats: THESE ARE Q4 POINT OBSERVATIONS, NOT ANNUAL AVERAGES — do not relabel them. EPI's tracker updates quarterly, so date-stamp anything taken from it. Verification performed: EPI's stated growth since 1979 is +93.2% productivity and +33.7% pay; 216.8 to 418.8 = +93.2% and 190.7 to 254.9 = +33.7%, both exact against the 1979Q4 and 2026Q1 rows.
productivity_pay_gap.mandatory_caveat: Ship causal-honesty note 7 with this chart. Stansbury & Summers (NBER w24165) find a one-point rise in productivity growth is associated with 0.7-1.0 points higher median/average compensation growth — the link is largely intact, and the divergence reflects forces acting on pay independent of productivity, not a broken link. EPI is a labor-aligned shop; label it.

union_density.label: Trade union membership as a percent of employed
union_density.critical_definitional_warning: THE DENOMINATOR HERE IS TOTAL EMPLOYED, NOT WAGE-AND-SALARY EMPLOYMENT. On this basis the 1950s peak is 28.3% (1954), NOT the commonly cited ~33%. The 33% figure uses union members as a share of NONAGRICULTURAL WAGE AND SALARY employment, a smaller denominator. IF THE 1950s ERA CARD SAYS 33%, IT MUST BE SOURCED SEPARATELY — do not cite this table for it. There is also a break at 1973 (23.7% to 21.3%) that is a source/denominator change, not a real one-year collapse.

bls_basis.note: BLS's own comparable series (wage and salary workers) starts 1983

home_price_to_income.label: Median home sale price to median household income
home_price_to_income.status: DERIVED — our arithmetic, not a published series
home_price_to_income.definition: Annual mean of the four quarterly MSPUS observations, divided by nominal median household income. BOTH inputs are nominal current dollars, so the ratio is apples-to-apples.

inputs.label: Median Sales Price of NEW Houses Sold

home_price_to_income.critical_caveat: MSPUS IS **NEW** HOUSES ONLY. JCHS's published ratio uses EXISTING single-family homes. New-home medians run above existing-home medians and are affected by builder product mix, so THIS IS NOT A SUBSTITUTE for the JCHS series and sits above it in level. Published JCHS values for comparison: 4.1 (2019) and 5.6 (2022) — this derived series gives 4.66 (2019) and 5.81 (2022).
home_price_to_income.other_caveats: MEHOINUSA646N has Census methodology breaks at 2013 and 2017-2019; the 2019 jump is partly a survey-processing artifact. Cannot start before 1984 because the nominal Census median household income series does not.
home_price_to_income.jchs_note: The full JCHS published series is .xlsx-blocked. The dossier's claimed '2.2-3.0 from 1950-1985' remains UNSOURCED — JCHS data starts in the early 1970s and the derived series here starts 1984.

abstract_wording.quote: We found that rates of absolute mobility have fallen from approximately 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s.

body_wording.quote: the fraction of children earning more than their parents fell from 92% in the 1940 birth cohort to 50% in the 1984 birth cohort

endpoints_conflict.RESOLUTION_REQUIRED: BOTH QUOTES ARE VERBATIM FROM THE SAME PAPER — the abstract rounds and generalizes, the body is precise. The dossier used 92%/1984, which Phase 0's first pass flagged as a secondary-retelling error; the second pass found it IS in the paper's body. USE 92% AND THE 1984 COHORT, citing the body, OR use ~90% and 'the 1980s', citing the abstract. Do not mix. This is a genuine correction to the Phase 0 provenance table.

top_income_share_piketty_saez_fiscal.label: Top income shares — Piketty-Saez FISCAL income (the original series)
top_income_share_piketty_saez_fiscal.definition: The classic Piketty-Saez series. Unit of observation is TAX UNITS, not equal-split adults. Income concept is FISCAL income (income reported on tax returns), NOT national income — it excludes undistributed corporate profits and imputed rents. Transfers excluded. Two capital-gains variants are stored: excluding realized capital gains, and including them.
top_income_share_piketty_saez_fiscal.source: Piketty & Saez QJE 2003, updated: Emmanuel Saez, TabFig2024.xlsx, Tables A1 (excluding capital gains) and A3 (including capital gains)
top_income_share_piketty_saez_fiscal.coverage: 1913-2024, 112 points — B7 CLOSED, extended from 1998 using Saez's TabFig2024.xlsx
top_income_share_piketty_saez_fiscal.caveats: TAX UNITS, fiscal income (income reported on tax returns), transfers excluded. A THIRD definition, distinct from WID/DINA and Auten-Splinter — never splice or average the three. Both capital-gains variants stored; the chart must label which it plots.
